content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Bun v1.4.5, released November 19, 2026, is what the [Bun blog](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4.5) calls "a security release," bumping five bundled dependencies: lsquic, c-ares, SQLite, llhttp and BoringSSL. The [post](https://bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4.5), written by Dylan Conway, says the fixes touch HTTP/3, HTTP/1.1, TLS, DNS and Zstandard, and lists the affected surface as "`Bun.serve`, `Bun.connect`, `Bun.dns`, `Bun.zstdDecompress`, `node:tls`, `node:https`, `node:http`, `node:quic`, `...

recommendations: Close the PR without merging. The work is discarded under the v3.9.0 workflow.

editor_notes.content_quality: Clean, well-structured News piece (726 words, within the 400-1200 range). Overview/What We Know/What We Don't Know structure is used correctly: the final section is a genuine disclosure of what the primary sources do not state (exploitation status, the undocumented first lsquic GHSA ID), not a recap. Technical explanation of the lsquic path-slot bug is accurate and clearly written for a developer audience.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 5 cited sources read from disk snapshots (gunzip'd .html.gz) except one, verified by an alternate route documented below. (1) source-0.html.gz (bun.com/blog/bun-v1.4.5, 200, sha256 2d28d73a...) confirms the Nov 19 2026 release, the 5 bundled-dependency version bumps (lsquic 4.9.4->4.11.2, c-ares 1.34.8->1.34.9, SQLite 3.53.4->3.54.1, llhttp 9.4.2->9.4.4, BoringSSL Aug->Nov 2026), the SQLite/ALTER TABLE and node:crypto/cert-validation bugfix text, and the 'Bun's bundled roots are not affected' quote -- all verbatim. (2) source-1.html.gz (github.com/oven-sh/bun/releases/tag/bun-v1.4.5, 200) confirms the Nov 19 publish date and tag. (3) source-2.html.gz (github.com/c-ares/c-ares/releases/tag/v1.34.9, 200) confirms 'This is a security release', the Oct 19 2026 date, and an exact count of 11 listed GHSA advisories (verified by manual enumeration of the release-note bullet list), plus verbatim matches for the 'A DNS reply that arrived from a different server...' and ares_dup()/ares_save_options() buffer-overflow quotes; no CVE identifiers appear anywhere in the release notes, confirming the article's 'None...carries a published CVE number' claim. (4) source-3.html.gz (github.com/litespeedtech/lsquic/releases/tag/v4.11.2, 200) confirms the Nov 16 2026 publish date (3 days before Bun's release, as the article states) and the verbatim 'Preserve validated paths when the path table is full, preventing undecryptable packets from redirecting queued traffic' fix line with both GHSA IDs. (5) github.com/litespeedtech/lsquic/security-advisories/GHSA-fg6p-g89q-65wr returned a genuine 404 at fetch time -- the cited URL path is malformed (the submission uses the old-style 'security-advisories' single segment; GitHub's actual path is 'security/advisories', a '/' not embedded in the word). I independently confirmed this by direct curl with a browser User-Agent to https://github.com/litespeedtech/lsquic/security/advisories/GHSA-fg6p-g89q-65wr (200, saved to /tmp/ghsa.html, 167202 bytes) and by checking that no Archive.org capture exists for the broken URL. The corrected-URL page verbatim confirms: 'One 49-byte datagram that carries the server's connection ID and cannot be decrypted then made the server send 10265 bytes (209.5x) to its source address, which was never validated' (exact match to the article's blockquote), 'No known CVE', and the term 'path slots' used by the article. The one mismatch: the page's own severity label reads 'Severity Moderate / 5.8 CVSS' -- GitHub's four-tier UI label is 'Moderate', not the article's 'medium severity'. The CVSS 4.0-6.9 band is conventionally called 'Medium' under the generic CVSS qualitative scale, so this is defensible as a synonym and not a factual error, but it doesn't match the source's own displayed word, so I note it rather than silently passing it. Figure/count re-verification requested by the orchestrator: the 209.5x amplification figure and the 'eleven' c-ares advisory count were both independently recomputed from the raw GitHub release-note/advisory text (not taken from the submission's own arithmetic) and both check out exactly. Quote-by-quote audit: every one of the 12 double-quoted spans in body_markdown was traced to its cited source and matched verbatim (case and wording) -- the two case-mismatch quotes and the one bracket-modified quote the writer reports self-correcting are not present in the final submitted text; no residual quote-fidelity issues found. Cross-reference check: the internal link to /article/2026-10/22-nodejs-security-releases-... resolves to an existing published article, and that article's own body confirms Node.js bundled the same c-ares 1.34.9 in its Oct 21 2026 releases, so the 'Bun is not the first runtime' claim is accurate and this is not a duplicate story (different subject, only a one-sentence cross-reference). Anthropic disclosure: required - source-0.html.gz (bun.com's own page footer) reads 'The fast all-in-one JavaScript runtime & toolkit. Now part of Anthropic.' / 'Bun x Anthropic' / 'Baked with (heart) in San Francisco . (c) 2026 Anthropic, PBC' -- Bun is confirmed to be an Anthropic-owned product per editorial_policy.md's own example list ('Claude Code or Bun'), and this article's headline/lead is about Bun. No sentence disclosing that the Herald's contributor model is built by Anthropic appears anywhere in the submission. This is a required disclosure that is missing, filed below as a clarification record per policy section 'Disclosure of the contributor model's maker'.
